PCM-catalysed protein methylation reactions are not of primary regulatory importance for the motility of sperms, but that the high activity of PCM in sperms and the presence of a large number of D-aspartate residues in sperm proteins suggest that PCM-catalyzation of D-aspartic acid residues may be of considerable significance for the maintenance of sperm motility and viability.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
protein O-carboxy- l methyltransferase in spermatozoa may be a repair enzyme for proteins that have undergone spontaneous racemization.

protein O-carboxy- methyltransferase in mammalian spermatogenic cells and spermatozoa appears to catalyze a process of protein methylesterification that is of unknown significance, but which does not seem to be of regulatory significance for male gamete production or function.

the PCM-catalyized methylesterification reaction in mammalian sperms is a non-regulatory process that is probably of little significance for their motility, and that the high PCM activity in sperms is related to a special need for repair and disposal of D-aspartate-containing proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
protein O-carboxy-methyltransferase activity of sperms is high and may be related to the disposal or repair of damaged proteins.
the methyl esters of D-aspartate in rat and human sperm proteins are hydrolyzed rapidly and spontaneously at physiological and especially at higher pH values.
protein O-carboxymethylation is a ubiquitous and abundant modification in mammalian spermatozoa, but the physiological significance of this modification remains unknown.
